pages.title: How Wales captain Dewi Lake's rousing speech inspired historic win against All Blacks - BBC Sport
pages.description: Dewi Lake's rousing team talk helped ensure Wales did not let the chance to make history against New Zealand slip away.
pages.text: How Wales captain Dewi Lake's rousing speech inspired historic win against All Blacks - BBC Sport Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, Dewi Lake has captained Wales 24 times Published 16 November 2026 Inside the Wales dressing room at the Principality Stadium at half-time on Saturday, heads could easily have bowed. Visitors New Zealand had just levelled the scores at 21-21 with the clock in the red at the end of the first half. It was a sucker punch that could have knocked the wind out of Welsh sails. But captain Dewi Lake summoned the words that inspired a first win over New Zealand in 73 years. With a rousing speech, the captain reminded his players of the feeling in the same changing room 12 months earlier, when they trailed by just three points at the break only to eventually lose 52-26. "Dewi made a very good point, the last time that we played them we had been in the contest, but let the dam break," Leicester and Wales wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb told the Rugby Union Weekly podcast. "They slipped through and we promised ourselves that we weren't going to let that happen again, that we had an opportunity to really do something special. "The heart the boys showed from then on, we wanted it more than they did. New Zealand were shocked and there was no way that we were going to let it slip." You can try some simple forms of it in a meeting, on a flight or while reading this article. It can be easy to spend an entire day sitting. First at your desk at work, then perhaps in your car, followed by a couple of hours on the sofa. Before you know it, you're having dinner and realise you haven't exercised all day. Many global studies have found that a sedentary lifestyle can increase the risk of serious health conditions . Everything we can do to decrease sedentary time therefore benefits our overall health. But it can be challenging to find the time. That's where incidental exercise comes in. This is the moving around we do outside of deliberate exercise. It's also known as "non-exercise activity thermogenesis", or NEAT. This refers to any energy we use for movement that isn't sleeping, eating or deliberate exercise, says Anantha Narayanan, a research fellow at the Auckland University of Technology in New Zealand. Help for Survey Participants How We Conduct Our Surveys In addition to conducting the decennial census count, the Census Bureau conducts various surveys that study households, businesses, schools, hospitals, and more. The Census Bureau will notify you in advance if you are in a survey, provide different ways to respond, and may follow up with you. We notify you if you are in a survey. The U.S. Census Bureau typically sends an official letter describing the survey for which your household or business has been selected and why your participation is important. This letter describes what the survey is, what type of questions will be asked, and what you can expect as a survey participant. For household surveys, most mailings from the Census Bureau are addressed to “the resident of.” Household surveys from the Census Bureau are only mailed to residential addresses, not to P.O. Boxes. P.O. Boxes are not associated with specific addresses, so the Census Bureau cannot use them as a mailing destination. If you are visited by a field representative working on a survey and have not yet received a survey letter or notice from the Census Bureau, you can request one from the representative at your door. You may also contact the Census Bureau Regional Office for your state for more information. Some surveys send invitations via text message or email. You can verify an email or text message is from the Census Bureau by noting the email address or phone number from which the invitation was sent.

While resale sites are growing in popularity, in the UK we still bin about 711,000 tonnes of textiles annually – roughly the weight of seven US aircraft carriers . The global fashion and textiles industry is one of the most wasteful, but recycling firms in Peterborough and Northamptonshire are using technology to change that. They are gaining the attention of major brands but say they need laws, as well as consumers, to support them. A facsimile of the Trojan Horse in the port city of Çanakkale, Türkiye, draws travelers and fans of the epic Greek poems. dinosmichail, Alamy By Nick Hilden Published July 17, 2026 Driving south out of the petite port town of Çanakkale, on the northwestern tip of Türkiye, signs for “Truva” and “Troya” begin to appear with growing frequency. The bustle of modern life gives way to the pastoral, and half an hour later, you’re in the ancient city of Troy, some 3,000 years in the past. A towering wooden horse greets you at the gate and all around are scattered ruins, the Aegean Sea in the distance, and the plains upon which the legendary Trojan War was fought in between. “The aura is so strong, [that] when Caesar visited Troy he said, ‘Every stone has a name,’” says Rüstem Aslan , a professor at Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University , who has spent 40 years excavating the UNESCO World Heritage site believed to be the legendary city. Today, Hisarlik—Turkish for “ place of fortresses ,” the name for the hill where the ruins lie—recounts its history through the Troy Museum and the remains of architectural structures containing the echoes of Homer ’s great epic, The Odyssey . pages.text: Human jaws are surprisingly strong and efficient | National Geographic SCIENCE NOT EXACTLY ROCKET SCIENCE Human jaws are surprisingly strong and efficient By Ed Yong Published June 22, 2010 • 4 min read Stephen Wroe has built a career out of analysing some of the planet’s most formidable skulls. His group at the University of New South Wales have studied the strength, sturdiness and biting power of the sabre-toothed cat , the great white shark , and the Komodo dragon . Now, he has turned his attention to a predator whose skull is far less impressive but yields surprises all the same – us. Humans, it is said, have relatively weak jaws that can’t inflict or withstand high bite forces. Some have suggested that we are adapted to eat foods that aren’t very tough, or that our use of tools and cooking has lessened the evolutionary pressure on maintaining sturdy jaws. Some have even suggested that our weedy jaw muscles made way for our large brains and thus facilitated their evolution. But according to Wroe, all of these explanations have a fatal flaw – our jaws aren’t weak at all. They’re actually remarkably efficient for a primate. The notion of weak human chops was based on very unrefined models that treated our jaws as two-dimensional levers. Of course, in real life, we chew in three glorious dimensions. To really understand how strong our mandibles are, we need to add that third dimension to the models. That’s exactly what Wroe did. He used his signature technique, called finite element analysis , to create a virtual model of a human skull (belonging to a San hunter-gatherer).

pages.text: Humans used to have straighter teeth—what changed? | National Geographic HEALTH Humans used to have straighter teeth—what changed? New research explores how diet, evolution, and facial anatomy may have shaped our modern smiles. Studies of ancient skulls show wider jaws and fewer malocclusions, leading researchers to explore how diet and lifestyle shaped the human face. Photograph by Alan/Adobe Stock By Leah Worthington Published July 15, 2025 Braces, rubber bands, even jaw surgery—millions endure them in pursuit of a straighter smile. But were misaligned smiles always this common? Research suggests that might not be the case. While malocclusions—crowded or misaligned teeth—have been found among our hunter-gatherer ancestors, they appear to be more prevalent in modern populations. So what changed? Experts say the answer isn’t simple but point to one possible culprit: our diets. As we traded raw, tough foods for softer, more processed ones, the burden of chewing decreased, allowing our jaws to shrink over time. Now, researchers are exploring how evolutionary biology, diet, and modern lifestyles may have reshaped our faces—and our smiles. How farming may have reshaped the human face Ancient human skulls were strikingly different from our own. Early hunter-gatherers had large, powerful jaws built for the demanding work of chewing tough meats, fibrous vegetables, seeds, and nuts. But around 12,000 years ago, things began to change. pages.text: Hundreds still homeless after 'unsafe' Canning Town flats evacuation Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Hundreds still homeless after being evacuated from 'unsafe' flats 4 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Ayshea Buksh London BBC The Royal Gateway, also known as Caxton Works, was advertised as "an exciting regeneration project" when it was built Hundreds of residents in east London remain homeless after structural defects were discovered at an award-winning high-rise development that was declared "at risk of sudden collapse". The Royal Gateway, also known as Caxton Works in Canning Town, Newham, was built less than 10 years ago. But last month, people living there were suddenly told to leave - some in the middle of the night by London Fire Brigade - because it was "unsafe". Businesses renting commercial spaces were also told to evacuate their premises. Engineers identified concerns with reinforced concrete "transfer slabs" supporting the buildings - an issue that has emerged at other London developments, prompting wider scrutiny of the construction method. Property company Galliard Homes, which built the scheme, says it is working to "investigate the concerns and develop potential solutions", while giving financial and practical support to residents. pages.text: Hungary v Northern Ireland: We want to play on the biggest stages - Isaac Price - BBC Sport Image source, Press Eye Image caption, West Brom midfielder Isaac Price has started Northern Ireland's last 25 matches By Andy Gray BBC Sport NI Journalist Published 16 November 2026 When Northern Ireland step out into the Puskas Arena on Tuesday night, they hope it will be a taste of what is to come. In the 70,000-seater stadium, which hosted the Champions League final between Paris St-Germain and Arsenal in May, Northern Ireland's destiny will be in their own hands. In 18 months' time, Michael O'Neill's young side will hope be at the Euro 2028 finals. But for now, they face Hungary with hopes of promotion to League A in the Nations League for the first time. A win or a draw will do the job in Budapest, and it would be the latest step for a Northern Ireland side who continue to show encouraging signs in their development. Worst case, NI will still have a shot at a play-off for League A in March but their sole aim is to get the job done on Tuesday. Midfielder Isaac Price, who has grown into a key player under O'Neill, says you "have got to love the expectation". "That's what you play football for. We're playing in a stadium where 70,000 people will be watching and then there'll be loads more at home watching," he told BBC Sport NI. "That's what you grow up and want to do. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson. In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase". But the Wrap praised its "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best." Hydraulic Properties The Office of Geothermal’s Innovative Methods to Control Hydraulic Properties of Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) , or Hydraulic Properties, initiative supports the research, development, demonstration, and deployment of technologies and techniques to control the fluid flow within the fracture network in EGS reservoirs in order to optimize them for heat extraction. EGS systems use human-made reservoirs to access subsurface heat where natural subsurface conditions lack sufficient fluid flow—or permeability—or water to allow heat to be drawn to the surface for energy. Projects under this initiative are developing targeted and reversible in-reservoir fracture permeability modification systems or methods and yield long-term reservoir productivity improvements. The ability to customize reservoirs via these methods will increase reservoir efficiency and longevity, ultimately helping to drive down EGS costs, reduce the risk of development, and accelerate the path towards widespread commercialization. Hydrothermal Resources What Are Hydrothermal Resources? The natural formation of a hydrothermal resource requires three principal elements: heat, water, and permeability. When water is heated in the earth, hot water or steam is trapped in porous and fractured rocks beneath a layer of relatively impermeable caprock, resulting in the formation of a hydrothermal reservoir. If the conditions underground are right, humans can harness that geothermal hot water or steam by drilling and then bring it to the surface to generate electricity . These types of geothermal systems typically occur close to tectonic plate boundaries, like in the western portions of the United States. Sometimes the resource is easy to find because of indicators on the surface like hot springs. Other times, conventional geothermal resources are “ hidden ,” with no signs of the underground reservoir on the surface. Hydrothermal resources are considered conventional geothermal resources because they can be developed using existing technologies and do not require creation of human-made reservoirs as needed with enhanced geothermal systems . Practicing good hygiene is a core prevention strategy recommended for everyone to lower your risks from respiratory illnesses. Recommendation Practice good hygiene by covering your coughs and sneezes, washing or sanitizing your hands often, and cleaning frequently touched surfaces. How it works Covering your coughs and sneezes limits the spread of germs to protect others. Handwashing with soap removes germs from your hands, making them less likely to infect your respiratory system when you touch your eyes, nose, or mouth. If soap and water are not available, using a hand sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol can kill these germs. To remove germs and dirt on surfaces, use household cleaners that contain soap or detergent. Steps you can take Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue when you cough or sneeze . pages.description: Dylan Thomas’s Under Milk Wood reminded me of my dad’s decency and mischief. I laughed as I cried, and realised there’s no right way to go through the grieving process
pages.text: I felt nothing but numbness at my dad’s death – but then I read the book he gave me on my wedding day | Culture | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The Guardian My cultural awakening Culture I felt nothing but numbness at my dad’s death – but then I read the book he gave me on my wedding day Dylan Thomas’s Under Milk Wood reminded me of my dad’s decency and mischief. I laughed as I cried, and realised there’s no right way to go through the grieving process Ioan Marc Jones Sat 14 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Last modified on Sat 14 Nov 2026 10.39 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I expected to break. But I felt nothing. I did not cry, nor struggle to sleep. I seldom thought of him. I felt only guilt about how little I felt. Ours was a complex relationship. As a teen, I often resented my dad, occasionally despised him. I expected the world and found disappointment. But, as I grew older, I understood that he had struggles of his own. I learned to appreciate his decency and humour, his ability to make everyone laugh with only a few words. I loved my dad, from the first time he held me to the last time I held him. But still, as weeks turned into months, I struggled to grieve. Then, when my partner and I rearranged our bookshelves, I found the first edition of Under Milk Wood that my parents gave us on our wedding day. I turned the cover and saw the note: “And all the bells of the tills of the town shall ring for our wedding.” It was my mum’s writing, but my dad’s idea.

A cancer diagnosis can disrupt your diabetes management and your eating plan. Find out how cancer treatment can affect your blood sugar, and get tips to help you get the nutrition you need. Cancer treatment and your blood sugar Chemotherapy , or chemo, helps kill or shrink cancer cells, but it also hurts some healthy cells. This can cause side effects, like mouth sores, nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite. These side effects may make it hard to eat, which could cause low blood sugar. Radiation therapy kills cancer cells by using high-energy rays. Radiation therapy causes your body to release extra sugar to help cope with the treatment. This reaction can cause a spike in your blood sugar. Radiation can also cause fatigue, which may make it harder to stick to your meal and activity plans. pages.text: ICC criticised for 'disrespectful' changes to World Cup by Cricket Scotland and KNCB - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Richie Berrington and Bas de Leede are the current captains of Scotland and the Netherlands respectively By Timothy Abraham BBC Sport Journalist Published 10 August 2026 The cricket boards of Scotland and the Netherlands have criticised the International Cricket Council for structural changes made to the men's 50-over World Cup. Last month the ICC announced the main part of the tournament for 2027 would be 12 teams in two groups of six, rather than 14 as originally planned. The three lowest-ranked qualifiers will instead be placed in a preliminary three-team Super Series, from which only the winner will progress. It effectively means the likes of Scotland and the Netherlands could face three qualifying tournaments to reach the main group stage of the World Cup. A joint statement from Cricket Scotland and Royal Dutch Cricket Association (KNCB) said they had "significant concerns" about the "impact of these changes" along with the "process through which they have been introduced". "The changes risk weakening the integrity and credibility of international cricket, and only highlights the importance of strong governance, transparent decision-making and effective engagement with members," the statement said. "Changing those structures at short notice creates significant uncertainty, disrupts planning, and places additional operational and financial pressure on organisations that are already operating with limited resources." Read our June 2026 story Most people think of lions as strictly African beasts, but only because they've been killed off almost everywhere else. Ten thousand years ago lions spanned vast sections of the globe, and so did people, who—as they multiplied and organized—put pressure on competitors at the top of the food chain. Now lions hold only a small fraction of their former habitat, and Asiatic lions, a subspecies that split from African lions perhaps 100,000 years ago, hang on to an almost impossibly small slice of their former domain. India is the proud steward of these 300 or so lions, which live primarily in a 560-square-mile sanctuary. Energy.gov April 3, 2025 Estimated Read Time min GOLDEN, COLORADO— U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright received strong support from the Department of Energy’s (DOE) National Lab and nuclear weapons assembly plant directors after he announced expedited permitting reforms for construction projects on Energy Department lands. These common sense reforms will save at least hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars and rapidly accelerate project completion dates, helping better unleash American innovation, restore energy dominance, and modernize America’s nuclear stockpiles.
